title: The Invisible Gorilla
text:
In 1999 Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris, then at Harvard University, filmed a short video of two teams of students passing basketballs, one team in white shirts and the other in black. Viewers were asked to count the passes made by the white team, a task that required close attention.

About halfway through the clip, something strange happened. In one version, a woman carrying an open umbrella walked through the game. In another, a person in a full gorilla suit walked into the middle of the players, stopped, faced the camera, thumped its chest and walked off.

After the video, the researchers asked whether viewers had noticed anything unusual. About half of them had not seen the gorilla at all. When they were shown the clip again, many could hardly believe they had missed it, and some suspected the researchers had switched tapes. The harder the counting task, the more people missed it.

Simons and Chabris used the study to illustrate inattentional blindness, a phenomenon earlier studied by Ulric Neisser and by Arien Mack and Irvin Rock: when our attention is focused on one task, we can fail to see something obvious that we are not looking for. Just as striking, people are confident that they would notice such things. The experiment has been repeated many times and became one of the best known demonstrations in psychology.
lesson: Focus has a price: what you are not looking for, you may not see at all. When much is at stake, ask someone with a different focus to look at the same situation.
source: Simons, D. J., and Chabris, C. F. (1999). Gorillas in our midst: Sustained inattentional blindness for dynamic events. Perception, 28(9), 1059-1074.
